blocks.#page-guide .guide-body:
This archive records who named each plant, when and where, with a source for every claim. This page explains how names are written, how to read a record and how to post. Definitions are in the glossary.

Kinds and how names are written

Each name shows two things: where the plant comes from (Species, Hybrid or Unknown) and whether the name means one single plant (Clone). Both are shown side by side, as in "Hybrid · Clone".

Species
A species formally published under a scientific name. We check the author, year and publication in IPNI and POWO and record the type locality and distribution. For a synonym, the accepted name is shown on the label too. Examples: Anthurium warocqueanum T.Moore (1878), Anthurium sagittatum (Sims) G.Don (a name made by a transfer).
Undescribed
A plant with no published name, or one not yet identified. It carries sp. (species not determined), aff. (close to a known species but thought different) or cf. (probably that species, to be confirmed), and a provisional name goes in " ". We never invent a name. Examples: Anthurium sp. "Peru", Anthurium aff. besseae, Anthurium sp. "antolakii" (unpublished name).
Hybrid
The name of a plant made by crossing. We write the cross, or say that the parents are unknown or complex. Without the Clone mark, the name is shared by many plants from the same cross. Examples: 'Dark Mama' (every plain warocqueanum × papillilaminum cross takes this name), 'BVIT' (a trade label used on plants of different parents; no breeder applies).
Unknown
A name with no source that says whether it is a wild species or a cross. We do not call it a Hybrid on a guess, and we change it when a source turns up. Example: 'Ace of Spades' (Unknown · Clone).
Clone
A mark for a name held only by one plant (the original) and the plants grown from it by division or tissue culture. It can go with Species, Hybrid or Unknown. Seedlings (F plants) are different plants; if F plants are sold under the same name, the name also gets the "line" mark. Examples: 'Mystique A88' (Hybrid · Clone), 'King of Spades' (Unknown · Clone; the original is a single plant of Haji Ulih, plants on the market are F plants).
Species · Clone
A number or name given to one plant of a species (a numbered individual). It is normally written with the species epithet, but it can be listed without one when the species is not known. It appears among the Clones and in the "Individuals" section of that species' page. Examples: A. papillilaminum 'Fort Sherman', A. carlablackiae 'HR1'.
Seedling
A record of seeds you sowed yourself, told apart by the cross, the sowing date and the breeder. Once you name the plants and give them out, register them separately as a Hybrid (Hybrid · Clone if the name means one plant). Signed in, you can keep as many as you like for free, and make them private.

When unsure, in this order: 1. A plant with a scientific name, or a wild species-level plant → Species (Undescribed if no name has been published). 2. A source says it came from a cross → Hybrid. 3. No source either way → Unknown (never Hybrid on a guess). 4. Unless a source says the name covers the whole cross or a group of seedlings, add the Clone mark (a name points to the original plant). 5. Your own sowing with no name → Seedling.

Three kinds of "not known": an empty line on the label is written one of three ways. "Not recorded" = not checked yet. "Not given in the protologue (sine loc.)" = the original description was read and does not say. "Not applicable" = the item does not exist (such as the breeder of a trade label).

Quotation marks: cultivar names, individual names and trade names take single quotes ('King of Spades', 'HR1'). Informal species-level names take double quotes (sp. "Peru"). Published epithets take none. Put a space before and after ×.

Reading a record

Specimen label
The table under the name. For a species: author, year, collector, type locality and distribution; for a cross: breeder, year and cross. It is the summary.
Record heading
The sourced records under the photos. A heading such as "Source S · 95% · 2026.04.02" gives the source tier (S to D), the trust score and the date of the record. The source's name is under "Sources" below. Records are listed by trust, highest first.
Contributor's record · no source
A record written by the grower or breeder themselves, with no source URL. It gets no trust number. If you think it is wrong, vote "Doubt" or let us know through "Report".
AI draft
AI-written text with no source and low trust is folded and marked "Draft". It does not count as a record.
Incomplete record
The name is registered but the required items for its kind (author, year and source; cross and breeder; sowing date and so on) are not all there. A dotted sheet lists what is missing, and "Add a record" fills it in.
Verified
The "✓ Verified" mark on a record that an administrator has checked against IPNI or another source. The date is the day it was checked.

Posting

  1. Sign in with Google (no sign-in is needed to browse).
  2. From "+ Post" in the header, enter the genus, the kind and the name. For a species, entering the scientific name fills in the author, year and distribution (IPNI / POWO / WCVP). For a Clone, an AI search of the web runs once when it is registered.
  3. Only photos taken by the grower may be posted. After registering, add as many as you like with "Add photo" on the page.
  4. On an existing page, "Add a record" adds a sourced record. You can also fill in items one by one.
  5. On a species page, "Add individual" records the number or name of your own plant.
  6. If you doubt something, use "Request a re-check". Once an administrator approves it, the AI research runs again.

Printing specimen labels

On a plant page, "More" → "Print label" prints up to 8 labels on an A4 sheet, each with the name, author or breeder, year, locality, verification line and a QR code to the page (sign-in required). The QR code only points to this site's plant pages.

Pricing

Browsing, posting, the seedling notes and label printing are all free. There is no paid membership. Where the running costs come from is on Pricing and services.
blocks.#page-glossary .glossary-body:
Scientific names and descriptions

Scientific name
A Latin name made of the genus and the species epithet (e.g. Anthurium crystallinum). The genus starts with a capital, and both are written in italics.
Description (protologue)
The first scientific publication of a species as new. That publication is the protologue. "Year" on this site is the year the protologue was published.
Author
The person who published the scientific name, added after it in short form (e.g. T.Moore, Croat). An author in brackets (e.g. (Sims) G.Don) first published it in another genus or species; the one outside the brackets moved it to the present name.
Type specimen · type locality
The specimen chosen as the standard for the name, and the place it was collected. The type locality is where the species was first found, not its whole range.
Collector
The person who collected the type specimen, recorded on the specimen label with the collection number. When the type is a cultivated plant, the first person to collect it in the wild may differ from the collector of the specimen.
Distribution (habitat)
The range where the plant is known to grow wild. It is usually wider than the type locality.
Synonym · former spelling
Another scientific name or spelling used for the same plant in the past (e.g. debilis → debile). This site keeps them under "Other names and spellings".

Marks for unidentified and related plants

sp.
A plant whose species is not determined (short for species). The locality or source is added in double quotes (e.g. Anthurium sp. "Peru"). We never guess a name for it.
aff.
A plant close to a known species but thought to be a different one (affinis). Example: Anthurium aff. besseae.
cf.
A plant thought to be a known species but not confirmed (confer). Used when it is more likely that species than with aff.
ssp. / var. / f.
Subspecies, variety and form (forma): ranks below species. Not the same as a horticultural cultivar.
Locality form (ecotype)
A typical look found in the plants of one area within a species. It is told apart by adding the locality, as in Monstera obliqua "Peru", but it is not a cultivar name of its own.

Crosses and cultivars

Cross (formula)
Written as mother × father: the mother (seed parent) first, with a space before and after × (e.g. Anthurium forgetii × Anthurium 'Titanium').
F1 / F2 / self
F1 is the first generation from a cross, F2 the second (F1 crossed with F1), and self means seedlings from a plant pollinated with its own pollen.
Original · selected plant
The one plant picked from a group of seedlings and given a name. The name points to that original plant; its seedlings (F plants) are not the original even when sold under the same name.
Clone
Plants grown from one individual by division, cuttings or tissue culture; genetically the same. On this site it is the mark for a name that means one single plant, and it can go with Species, Hybrid or Unknown (e.g. Hybrid · Clone). See also the kinds in the guide.
Hybrid
A plant made by crossing, in that sense here too. A Hybrid without the Clone mark is a name for many plants from the same cross, and plants with the same name differ genetically.
Unknown (kind)
The kind for a name with no source that says whether it is a wild species or a cross. We do not call it a Hybrid on a guess. A name for one single plant is written "Unknown · Clone".
Seedling
A plant grown from seed, and the record of it. On this site, hobbyists' sowing records are registered as "Seedling".
TC (tissue culture) · somaclonal variation
Growing plants from a piece of tissue in sterile culture. Changes that arise in culture are called somaclonal variation; variegated plants sometimes come about this way.
Trade name
A name given on the market, apart from the scientific or cultivar name (e.g. 'El Choco Red' = Philodendron rubrijuvenile). Once the proper name is known, it is shown first. The cultivated plant code does not put trade names in quotes, but this site follows trade usage, puts them in ' ' and notes "trade name".
Variegated (variegata)
A plant whose leaves lack chlorophyll in places, giving white or yellow patterns. It happens in species and clones alike, so it is shown with a tag, not as a kind.

Individuals, lines and what is listed

Individual
A number or name given to one plant of a species ('HR1' and so on). Its kind is "Species · Clone" and it is listed among the Clones. Plants grown from it by division or tissue culture are the same individual; its seedlings are different individuals and do not inherit the name. Individuals are listed in the "Individuals" section of the species page, by the person who numbered them. Numbers belong to each person: the same number from different people means different plants.
Line
A mark that seedlings (F plants) are also sold under the same name. Whether the name itself points to the original plant (the Clone mark) is shown by the kind; this mark only says that seedlings with the same name are around. Shown here with the tag line.
Code number
A number growers and collectors give to tell plants apart ('HR1', 'A88'). Written in single quotes like a cultivar name, with who gave it and when. A number alone does not say the species.
Incomplete record
There is a record, but the required items for its kind (author, year and source; cross and breeder; sowing date and so on) are not all there, so it has not passed the quality check. It is kept out of search engines and counts. "Add a record" fills it in.
AI draft
AI-written text with no source URL and a trust score under 40. It is shown folded and not counted as a record; it becomes one once a person's record or a source is added.

This site's scores

Trust
How reliable an origin record is, from 0 to 100. It starts from the source tier and moves with readers' votes.
Tier S to D
S: name databases and protologues (IPNI, POWO, GBIF, original papers) / A: scientific literature / B: specialist books, botanic gardens and specialist nurseries' own information / C: collectors and community / D: no source, not verified.
IPNI / POWO / GBIF
IPNI (International Plant Names Index) indexes scientific names and protologues, POWO (Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew) gives accepted names and distributions, and GBIF is a database of specimens and observations. Species authors, years and type localities are checked against them.
